exam-2-s2.title: A zinc-silver cell
exam-2-s2.html:
A galvanic cell is built at 25 °C from a zinc strip in 1.0 M Zn(NO₃)₂ and a silver strip in 1.0 M AgNO₃. The strips are joined by a wire through a voltmeter, and the solutions by a salt bridge of KNO₃(aq). F = 96,485 C/mol e⁻.

Standard reduction potentials at 25 °C
Half-reactionE° (V)
Ag⁺(aq) + e⁻ → Ag(s)+0.80
Cu²⁺(aq) + 2 e⁻ → Cu(s)+0.34
Zn²⁺(aq) + 2 e⁻ → Zn(s)−0.76

items.q: Standard enthalpies of formation: SO₂(g) −296.8 kJ/mol; SO₃(g) −395.7 kJ/mol. What is ΔH° for 2 SO₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2 SO₃(g)?
options: −197.8 kJ/mol
+197.8 kJ/mol
−98.9 kJ/mol
−692.5 kJ/mol

why.correct: ΔH° = Σ ΔH°f(products) − Σ ΔH°f(reactants) = 2(−395.7) − [2(−296.8) + 0] = −791.4 + 593.6 = −197.8 kJ/mol. O₂(g) is an element in its standard state, so its ΔH°f is 0.
options: Right: products minus reactants, each times its coefficient.
This is reactants minus products, which flips the sign.
This leaves out the coefficients of 2; it is ΔH° for one mole of SO₃.
This adds the two enthalpies of formation instead of subtracting reactants from products.

items.q: For H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2 HI(g), an equilibrium mixture at 700 K has [H₂] = 0.0220 M, [I₂] = 0.0220 M and [HI] = 0.156 M. What is Kc at 700 K?

options: Right: the coefficient 2 becomes the exponent on [HI].
This leaves [HI] unsquared. Each concentration is raised to the power of its coefficient.
This is reactants over products, 1/K.
This adds the reactant concentrations instead of multiplying them.

items.q: What volume of 0.150 M NaOH is needed to neutralize 20.0 mL of 0.120 M H₂SO₄ completely? (H₂SO₄ gives two H⁺ per formula unit.)

options: Right: two moles of OH⁻ for each mole of H₂SO₄.
This uses M₁V₁ = M₂V₂ as if the acid gave one H⁺. Each H₂SO₄ needs two OH⁻.
This puts the two molarities the wrong way round: 0.150 × 20.0 ÷ 0.120.
This divides by 2 instead of multiplying: the base must supply twice the moles of the acid.

items.q: What is the pH of the buffer?

options: Right: the base-to-acid ratio is 0.0050/0.010 = 0.50, and log 0.50 = −0.30.
This puts the acid on top of the ratio. Henderson-Hasselbalch uses [A⁻]/[HA], base over acid.
This uses ln instead of log: ln 0.50 = −0.69. The equation uses the base-10 logarithm.
pH = pKa only when the acid and base are equal in amount; here there is twice as much acid.

items.q: 1.0 mL of 1.0 M HCl is added to the buffer. What is the pH afterward?

why.correct: The HCl adds 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol H₃O⁺, which reacts with CH₃COO⁻: base 0.0050 → 0.0040 mol; acid 0.010 → 0.011 mol. pH = 4.74 + log(0.0040/0.011) = 4.74 − 0.44 = 4.30.
options: Right: the added acid turns some of the conjugate base into acetic acid, and the new ratio sets the pH.
This subtracts the added acid from CH₃COOH and adds it to CH₃COO⁻. Added H₃O⁺ is used up by the base, making more acid.
This is the pH of 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol of HCl in 76 mL of water, as if the buffer were not there.
A buffer resists a change in pH but does not stop it: the ratio of base to acid changes, so the pH drops a little.

items.q: Why does the pH change so little when the HCl is added?
options: The H₃O⁺ added reacts with CH₃COO⁻ to make CH₃COOH, so the ratio changes only slightly
CH₃COOH molecules react with the H₃O⁺ added and turn it back into water molecules
The H₃O⁺ added is diluted by the 75 mL of buffer, so its effect on the pH is small
The Ka of acetic acid rises so that the buffer can take up the H₃O⁺ that was added

why.correct: CH₃COO⁻ + H₃O⁺ → CH₃COOH + H₂O goes essentially to completion, so the strong acid is used up. Both buffer components stay present in similar amounts, and the pH, set by their ratio, moves only a little.
options: Right: the conjugate base neutralizes the added acid.
CH₃COOH is an acid; it does not react with another acid. The conjugate base, CH₃COO⁻, is what takes up the H₃O⁺.
Dilution alone would leave a pH near 1.9, as in plain water. The small change comes from the reaction with CH₃COO⁻.
Ka depends only on temperature; adding acid does not change it.

items.q: Which piece of glassware measures the 25.0 mL of CH₃COONa solution most precisely?
options: A 25.00 mL volumetric pipet
A 50 mL beaker
A 100 mL graduated cylinder
A 250 mL Erlenmeyer flask

why.correct: A volumetric pipet is made to deliver one volume to ±0.03 mL or so, far more precisely than the other choices.
options: Right: a pipet delivers its marked volume to two decimal places.
Beaker marks are rough guides, good to about 5%.
A 100 mL cylinder reads to about ±0.5 mL, and is less precise for 25 mL than a pipet made for that volume.
Flask marks are rough guides for mixing and swirling, not for measuring.

items.q: A first-order reaction has a half-life of 50.0 s. If [A]₀ = 0.800 M, what is [A] after 250. s?

options: Right: the concentration halves five times.
This divides by the number of half-lives (5). Each half-life halves what is left: divide by 2 five times, that is by 32.
This is four half-lives (0.800/16). 250. s ÷ 50.0 s = 5.
This is one half-life only. A first-order reaction keeps halving with the same half-life.

items.q: How many oxygen atoms are in 4.40 g of carbon dioxide, CO₂ (44.01 g/mol)?

why.correct: 4.40 g ÷ 44.01 g/mol = 0.100 mol CO₂; each molecule has 2 O atoms, so 0.200 mol O × 6.022 × 10²³ /mol = 1.20 × 10²³ O atoms.
options: Right: moles of CO₂, times 2 oxygen atoms per molecule, times Avogadro's number.
This is the number of CO₂ molecules. Each molecule has two oxygen atoms.
This counts all three atoms in each molecule, carbon included.
This multiplies by the molar mass instead of dividing by it.

items.q: 10.0 g of H₂ (2.016 g/mol) and 64.0 g of O₂ (32.00 g/mol) react: 2 H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2 H₂O(l). What mass of water (18.02 g/mol) can form?

why.correct: H₂: 10.0/2.016 = 4.96 mol, which needs 2.48 mol O₂; only 2.00 mol O₂ is present, so O₂ is limiting. 2.00 mol O₂ × (2 mol H₂O/1 mol O₂) × 18.02 g/mol = 72.1 g.
options: Right: O₂ runs out first, so it sets the amount of water.
This uses all the H₂, but there is not enough O₂ to react with it. Find the limiting reactant first.
This adds the two masses. Some H₂ (about 1.9 g) is left over, so not all the mass ends up as water.
This uses a 1 : 1 ratio of O₂ to H₂O. The equation makes 2 mol H₂O per mol O₂.

items.q: What is the partial pressure of H₂ in the buret?
options: 731 torr
752 torr
773 torr
21.1 torr

why.correct: The gas in the buret is H₂ mixed with water vapor, and together they balance the room pressure: P(H₂) = 752 torr − 21.1 torr = 730.9 torr, which is 731 torr.
options: Right: by Dalton's law the room pressure is the sum of the two partial pressures, so subtract the water vapor's share.
This is the total pressure of the gas mixture. Gas collected over water also contains water vapor, whose 21.1 torr must be taken out.
This adds the water vapor's pressure instead of subtracting it. The total, 752 torr, already includes the water vapor.
This is the partial pressure of the water vapor, not of the hydrogen.

items.q: How many moles of H₂ did the student collect?
options: 1.44 mol
Right: pressure in atm, volume in liters and temperature in kelvins, to match R.
This uses 752 torr, the total pressure. The hydrogen's own pressure is 752 − 21.1 = 730.9 torr.
This uses 23.0 for the temperature. The gas laws need kelvins: 23.0 °C + 273.15 = 296.15 K.
This leaves the volume in milliliters. With R in L·atm/(mol·K), 36.4 mL must be 0.0364 L.

items.q: A second student forgets to subtract the vapor pressure of water and uses 752 torr as the pressure of H₂. How does this affect that student's calculated moles of H₂?
options: Too high, because the pressure used includes the water vapor's share
Too low, because water vapor takes up part of the gas volume
Unaffected, because water vapor does not react with magnesium
Too low, because a larger pressure gives a smaller calculated volume

why.correct: n = PV/RT, so a pressure that is too large (752 torr instead of 730.9 torr) gives too many moles, with V, R and T unchanged.
options: Right: the extra 21.1 torr belongs to the water vapor, and n is proportional to P.
The volume measured is the volume of the whole mixture, and it is used correctly; the error is in the pressure, and it makes n larger.
Water vapor does not react, but its pressure is still part of the 752 torr. Leaving it in changes the calculation.
The volume is measured, not calculated. With V fixed, a larger P in n = PV/RT gives a larger n.

items.q: The student plans to repeat the experiment with 0.0700 g of magnesium under the same conditions. Which prediction about the procedure is correct?
options: About 73 mL of gas will form, more than the 50.00 mL buret can hold
About 36 mL of gas will form again, because the acid is in excess
About 73 mL of gas will form, and the 50.00 mL buret will collect it
About 18 mL of gas will form, because twice the gas is at twice the pressure

why.correct: Twice the magnesium gives twice the moles of H₂, so about 2 × 36.4 = 72.8 mL at the same temperature and pressure. That is more than the 50.00 mL buret holds, so the student needs less magnesium or a larger collecting tube.
options: Right: the volume of gas is proportional to the moles of magnesium, and 73 mL overflows a 50.00 mL buret.
The acid is in excess, so magnesium is the limiting reactant: doubling the magnesium doubles the hydrogen.
The volume is right, but a 50.00 mL buret holds only about 50 mL; the extra gas would bubble out.
The gas is collected at the room's pressure, which does not change. More moles at the same pressure take up more volume, not less.

items.q: What is the pH of 0.0250 M Ba(OH)₂ at 25 °C? (Ba(OH)₂ is a strong base.)

why.correct: Each Ba(OH)₂ gives two OH⁻: [OH⁻] = 0.0500 M. pOH = −log 0.0500 = 1.301, so pH = 14.000 − 1.301 = 12.699 (three decimal places for a concentration with three significant figures).
options: Right: two hydroxide ions per formula unit, then pH = 14.00 − pOH.
This uses [OH⁻] = 0.0250 M. Ba(OH)₂ releases two OH⁻ per formula unit.
This is the pOH. A basic solution at 25 °C has a pH above 7: subtract from 14.00.
This is −log 0.0250, which counts one OH⁻ per formula unit and stops at pOH.

items.q: 1.60 g of NaOH (40.00 g/mol) dissolves in water in a coffee-cup calorimeter, and the temperature of the 51.6 g of solution rises from 21.50 °C to 29.60 °C. Take c = 4.18 J/(g·°C). What is ΔH for dissolving NaOH?
options: −43.7 kJ/mol
+43.7 kJ/mol
−1.75 kJ/mol
−4.37 × 10⁴ kJ/mol

why.correct: q(solution) = (51.6 g)(4.18 J/(g·°C))(8.10 °C) = 1.75 × 10³ J = 1.75 kJ. The solution warmed, so dissolving released that energy: ΔH = −1.75 kJ ÷ 0.0400 mol = −43.7 kJ/mol.
options: Right: per mole of NaOH, with a negative sign because the process released heat.
The solution got warmer, so the process released energy to it; ΔH for the process is negative.
This is the heat for 0.0400 mol, not per mole. Divide by the moles of NaOH.
This leaves q in joules and labels it kJ: 1,747 J is 1.747 kJ.

items.q: For 2 NO(g) + O₂(g) → 2 NO₂(g), rate = k[NO]²[O₂]. How does the initial rate change if [NO] is tripled and [O₂] is halved at the same time?
options: It increases by a factor of 4.5
It increases by a factor of 1.5
It increases by a factor of 9
It increases by a factor of 18

why.correct: The new rate is k(3[NO])²(½[O₂]) = 9 × ½ × k[NO]²[O₂] = 4.5 times the old rate.
options: Right: 3² for NO, times ½ for O₂.
This uses [NO] to the first power. The rate law squares [NO], so tripling it multiplies the rate by 9.
This leaves out the halving of [O₂], which is first order.
This doubles for O₂ instead of halving.

items.q: The molar solubility of silver chromate, Ag₂CrO₄, is 6.5 × 10⁻⁵ M at 25 °C. What is Ksp at 25 °C?

why.correct: Ag₂CrO₄(s) ⇌ 2 Ag⁺ + CrO₄²⁻, so [Ag⁺] = 2s and [CrO₄²⁻] = s. Ksp = (2s)²(s) = 4s³ = 4(6.5 × 10⁻⁵)³ = 1.1 × 10⁻¹².
options: Right: [Ag⁺] is twice the solubility, and it is squared.
This is s³: it squares [Ag⁺] but forgets that [Ag⁺] = 2s.
This is s², as if the salt gave one ion of each kind.
This is (2s)² only; the CrO₄²⁻ concentration, s, is left out.

items.q: A 0.10 M solution of acetic acid is diluted with water to 0.010 M at constant temperature. What happens to the percent of the acetic acid that is ionized, and why?
options: It increases: dilution makes Q smaller than Ka, so more acid ionizes
It decreases: with fewer acid molecules per liter, fewer can ionize
It stays the same: Ka is unchanged, so the same share ionizes
It increases: Ka becomes larger as the solution is diluted with water

why.correct: Diluting lowers [H₃O⁺], [CH₃COO⁻] and [CH₃COOH] by the same factor, so Q = [H₃O⁺][CH₃COO⁻]/[CH₃COOH] drops below Ka (two factors on top, one below). The net reaction goes forward, ionizing a larger fraction of the acid (about 1.3% at 0.10 M, 4.2% at 0.010 M).
options: Right: Q < Ka after dilution, so the ionization goes further.
The amount ionized per liter falls, but the fraction ionized rises.
Ka is unchanged, but the fraction ionized depends on the concentration too: the equilibrium has two particles on the product side for one on the reactant side.
Ka depends only on temperature, which is constant here.

items.q: A first-order reaction has k = 0.0231 min⁻¹. What is its half-life?
options: 30.0 min
43.3 min
60.0 min

why.correct: For a first-order reaction t½ = 0.693/k = 0.693/(0.0231 min⁻¹) = 30.0 min.
options: Right: the first-order half-life from the equations sheet.
This is 1/k, which leaves out the factor ln 2 = 0.693.
This multiplies 0.693 by k instead of dividing.
This is the time for two half-lives.

items.q: What is the pH of 0.10 M hypochlorous acid, HOCl (Ka = 3.0 × 10⁻⁸), at 25 °C?

options: Right: a weak acid ionizes only slightly, so [H₃O⁺] comes from the Ka expression.
This treats HOCl as a strong acid that ionizes completely.
This is the pKa of HOCl, not the pH of the solution.
This takes −log(Ka × C) and leaves out the square root.

items.q: What is the concentration of MnO₄⁻ in the diluted unknown?

why.correct: The line goes through the origin with slope εb = 0.098/(4.0 × 10⁻⁵ M) = 2.45 × 10³ M⁻¹. c = A/(εb) = 0.343/(2.45 × 10³ M⁻¹) = 1.40 × 10⁻⁴ M, which is 14.0 on the axis.
options: Right: A = εbc, read from the calibration line.
This reads 14.0 on the axis as 14.0 × 10⁻⁶ M. The axis unit is 10⁻⁵ M, so 14.0 means 1.40 × 10⁻⁴ M.
This multiplies the absorbance by εb instead of dividing by it.
Absorbance has no unit and is not a concentration; use the line to convert it.

items.q: What is the concentration of MnO₄⁻ in the stock solution?

why.correct: The stock was diluted from 10.0 mL to 50.0 mL, by a factor of 5, so it is 5 times more concentrated than the unknown: 5 × 1.40 × 10⁻⁴ M = 7.00 × 10⁻⁴ M (M₁V₁ = M₂V₂).
options: Right: undo the fivefold dilution.
This divides by the dilution factor. The stock is more concentrated than the diluted sample, not less.
This uses 50.0/40.0, the ratio of total volume to water added. The dilution factor is total volume over stock volume, 50.0/10.0.
This is the diluted unknown. The stock was diluted before it was measured.

items.q: What is the molar absorptivity, ε, of MnO₄⁻ at 525 nm?
options: 2.45 × 10³ M⁻¹ cm⁻¹

why.correct: The slope is εb = 0.098/(4.0 × 10⁻⁵ M) = 2.45 × 10³ M⁻¹. With b = 1.00 cm, ε = 2.45 × 10³ M⁻¹ cm⁻¹.
options: Right: slope divided by the path length.
This uses 4.0 instead of 4.0 × 10⁻⁵ M, leaving out the axis unit.
This is concentration divided by absorbance, the reciprocal of the slope.
This is the largest absorbance on the graph, not a slope.

items.q: The cuvette used for the unknown has a path length of 1.10 cm instead of 1.00 cm, but the student uses the calibration line above. How is the calculated concentration of the unknown affected?
options: Too high, because the longer path absorbs more light at the same concentration
Too low, because the light is spread over a longer path through the solution
Unaffected, because ε for MnO₄⁻ does not depend on the cuvette that is used
Too low, because more of the light passes through to reach the detector

why.correct: A = εbc, so at the same concentration a 10% longer path gives a 10% larger absorbance. Read on a line made with b = 1.00 cm, that absorbance gives a concentration about 10% too high.
options: Right: absorbance is proportional to path length.
A longer path means the light meets more absorbing ions, so the absorbance goes up, not down.
ε does not change, but b does, and the line assumes b = 1.00 cm.
A longer path lets less light through, which raises the absorbance.

items.q: For N₂(g) + 3 H₂(g) ⇌ 2 NH₃(g), Kc = 0.50 at a certain temperature. A flask at that temperature holds [N₂] = 0.10 M, [H₂] = 0.20 M and [NH₃] = 0.40 M. Which statement is correct?
options: Q = 200, so Q > K and the net reaction runs in reverse until Q = K
Q = 200, so Q > K and the net reaction runs forward until Q = K
Q = 20, so Q > K and K slowly rises until it is equal to Q
Q = 0.0050, so Q < K and the net reaction runs forward to make NH₃

why.correct: Q = [NH₃]²/([N₂][H₂]³) = (0.40)²/((0.10)(0.20)³) = 0.16/0.00080 = 200. Q > K, so there is too much product: the net reaction goes in reverse, using NH₃, until Q falls to K.
options: Right: Q > K means the net reaction makes reactants.
Q is right, but Q > K sends the net reaction toward reactants, not products.
This leaves out the exponents; and K does not change with concentration, only with temperature.
This is reactants over products, 1/Q.

items.q: What is E°cell for the zinc-silver cell?

why.correct: Silver ions are reduced (cathode) and zinc is oxidized (anode): E°cell = E°(cathode) − E°(anode) = +0.80 V − (−0.76 V) = +1.56 V.
options: Right: a galvanic cell has a positive E°cell.
This doubles the silver potential because the balanced equation has 2 Ag⁺. E° is intensive and is not multiplied by a coefficient.
This adds the two reduction potentials (0.80 + (−0.76)). Subtract the anode's reduction potential from the cathode's.
This takes zinc as the cathode. A galvanic cell runs in the direction with a positive E°cell.

items.q: What is ΔG° for Zn(s) + 2 Ag⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + 2 Ag(s)?
options: −301 kJ/mol
−151 kJ/mol
+301 kJ/mol
−3.01 × 10⁵ kJ/mol

why.correct: Two electrons are transferred per Zn: ΔG° = −nFE° = −(2 mol e⁻)(96,485 C/mol e⁻)(1.56 J/C) = −3.01 × 10⁵ J = −301 kJ per mole of reaction.
options: Right: n = 2, and 1 V = 1 J/C.
This uses n = 1. Each zinc atom gives up two electrons, and two Ag⁺ ions each take one.
A positive E°cell gives a negative ΔG°; the sign is lost here.
This is the value in joules labeled as kJ. Divide by 1,000.

items.q: What happens at the silver strip as the cell runs?
options: Ag⁺ ions gain electrons, and silver metal is deposited on the strip
Silver atoms lose electrons, and the strip slowly gets lighter
Zn²⁺ ions travel across to the strip and are reduced to zinc
Nitrate ions are reduced there, and a gas is given off at the strip

why.correct: Silver is the cathode: electrons arrive through the wire and reduce Ag⁺ from the solution, Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag, so silver plates onto the strip.
options: Right: reduction at the cathode deposits silver.
This is what happens at the zinc anode, where zinc is oxidized and the strip loses mass.
Zn²⁺ stays in its own beaker; the salt bridge carries K⁺ and NO₃⁻, and Ag⁺ is the species reduced here.
Ag⁺ (E° = +0.80 V) is much more easily reduced; the nitrate ions are spectators.

items.q: The silver half-cell is replaced with a copper strip in 1.0 M Cu(NO₃)₂. How does the cell potential change, and why?
options: It falls to +1.10 V, because Cu²⁺ is less easily reduced than Ag⁺
It rises, because each Cu²⁺ takes two electrons and each Ag⁺ only one
It stays at +1.56 V, because zinc is still the anode of the cell
It becomes −0.42 V, so the new cell no longer runs on its own

why.correct: E°cell = +0.34 V − (−0.76 V) = +1.10 V. Cu²⁺ has a lower reduction potential than Ag⁺ (+0.34 V against +0.80 V), so it pulls electrons less strongly and the cell potential is smaller.
options: Right: the cathode's reduction potential falls from +0.80 V to +0.34 V.
E° is intensive: the number of electrons per ion does not change the potential.
The anode is the same, but the cathode's reduction potential changed, and E°cell depends on both.
This computes E°(Cu) + E°(Zn) with a sign slip. Subtracting the anode's reduction potential gives +1.10 V.

items.q: Which species has bond angles closest to 120°?
options: NO₃⁻
NH₃
H₂O
CH₄

why.correct: The N in nitrate has three electron domains (its resonance structures each have one double and two single bonds) and no lone pair, so it is trigonal planar with 120° angles.
options: Right: three electron domains around N and no lone pair.
NH₃ has four electron domains, one a lone pair: trigonal pyramidal, about 107°.
H₂O has four electron domains, two of them lone pairs: bent, about 104.5°.
CH₄ has four bonding domains: tetrahedral, 109.5°.

items.q: What is the mass percent of nitrogen in ammonium sulfate, (NH₄)₂SO₄ (132.15 g/mol)? (N 14.01 g/mol)

why.correct: Each formula unit has 2 N atoms: 2 × 14.01 g = 28.02 g of N per 132.15 g, so the mass percent is 28.02/132.15 × 100% = 21.2%.
options: Right: count every N atom in the formula, then divide by the molar mass.
This counts one N atom; the subscript 2 outside the parentheses doubles the NH₄⁺.
This is the share of atoms (2 of 15) that are nitrogen, not the share of mass.
This divides the molar mass by the mass of nitrogen; the ratio is upside down.
